title: Asset Quality Review
summary: RBI review under Governor Raghuram Rajan forcing uniform recognition of stressed assets across banks, ending the Corporate Debt Restructuring practices that had concealed the twin balance sheet problem inherited from the 2004-2011 lending boom.
claimAtLaunch: Force honest recognition of bad loans so that resolution could begin, on the premise that a concealed problem cannot be fixed.
whatHappened: Reported PSB gross NPAs rose from 4.97% (March 2015) to a peak of 14.58% (March 2018) on the global-operations basis — a rise driven by recognition, not deterioration. Special dispensations for restructured loans were withdrawn and expected losses provided for. The combined loan book of banks under Prompt Corrective Action shrank around 11% between FY15 and FY18.
assessmentNote:
RESCORED FROM worked TO partly, 2026-08-06, and this record fails the independence test outright rather than on a technicality. The announcing body is the RBI. Every citation bearing on the claim is a Press Information Bureau release — a document produced in support of the claim, which the intra-state test excludes whoever computed the number inside it. The one routine-function source in the record, the RBI Financial Stability Report reached through credit-growth, does not bear on whether recognition was honest, and it is not held: it is cited through a news site’s account of the report, which the mirror rule grades T4. THE VERDICT IS NOT failed. Honest recognition may well have happened; on the evidence here it is UNESTABLISHED, and unestablished is not negative. What is independently established is narrower than the claim, which is what partly records.

PREVIOUS NOTE, PRESERVED VERBATIM: Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. WORKED IS ASSERTED ON RECOGNITION, WHICH IS WHAT WAS PROMISED, AND NOT ON THE CONSEQUENCES. The stated object was to force honest recognition so resolution could begin. That is measured and it happened: reported public-sector gross non-performing assets rose from 4.97 per cent in March 2015 to 14.58 per cent in March 2018 on a rise driven by recognition rather than deterioration, special dispensations were withdrawn, and losses were provided for. A measure whose object is to reveal a number succeeds when the number is revealed. THE COST SIDE IS ARGUED AND NOT MEASURED. The case against holds that simultaneous recognition under lending constraints contributed meaningfully to the growth deceleration from 8 to 3.9 per cent; no decomposition separating that contribution from the other causes exists in anything retrieved, and it is entered below as an absence. A reader should take this verdict as saying the disclosure objective was met, NOT that the sequencing was costless.
caseFor: This was the precondition for everything that followed — IBC referrals, recapitalisation, and the eventual cleanup all required knowing the true scale. Every year of delay would have compounded the cost, as the 2004-2011 concealment had already demonstrated. The IMF and most academic assessment regard recognition as correct and overdue, and the subsequent trajectory to a 1.8% ratio by 2026 vindicates the sequencing.
caseAgainst: The execution was arguably too abrupt. Forcing recognition across the system simultaneously, while PCA constraints bound the affected banks, precipitated a credit squeeze at a moment when private investment was already weak — a meaningful contributor to the pre-COVID growth deceleration from 8% to 3.9%. A more graduated recognition schedule might have achieved the same honesty while preserving credit flow.
differentFactsNote: The government's case rests on recognition being the precondition for every step that followed, and on the compounding cost of continued concealment. The critics' case rests on the credit contraction that followed and its contribution to the pre-COVID deceleration. Netting the two would require the cost of the concealment that did not happen, which is a counterfactual rather than a measure - unobservable in principle, not merely unbuilt.

shockExposure.why: The 2018 IL&FS collapse hit as recognition peaked, compounding the credit squeeze and making the AQR's independent contribution to the slowdown hard to isolate.
Demonetisation and GST also landed inside this window.

unmeasured.what: The share of the pre-COVID growth deceleration attributable to the recognition exercise and the lending constraints that accompanied it
unmeasured.why: The case against turns on this and no decomposition exists in anything retrieved. Separating a credit-supply contraction's contribution to growth from contemporaneous demand, global and investment-cycle causes requires a counterfactual for which no agreed construction exists.

sources.name: PIB, GNPA of PSBs declined from the peak of 14.58%

title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code
summary: A unified insolvency framework drafted by the Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee, creating the NCLT and NCLAT adjudicatory architecture and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, and shifting control of a defaulting firm from promoter to creditor.
claimAtLaunch: Time-bound resolution within 180 days, extendable to 270 and later capped at 330 days including litigation, replacing a fragmented recovery regime that recovered little and took years.
whatHappened: 8,987 corporate debtors admitted since inception. Cumulative realisation stands at 30.56% of admitted claims (March 2026), down from 32.76% a year earlier and around 45% in the early years — ₹3.99 lakh crore realised against ₹12.31 lakh crore admitted, a roughly 67% haircut. Average resolution time worsened to 713 days (March 2025) and around 744 days on ICRA's 2025-26 estimate, versus the 330-day statutory limit. FY2025-26 annual-flow realisation fell to about 23%. Landmark resolutions included Essar Steel, Bhushan Steel, Electrosteel, DHFL and Ruchi Soya; Videocon and Jaypee Infratech were the notable controversies. The 2025 Amendment Bill, passed by the Lok Sabha on 31 March 2026, introduced a creditor-initiated process, mandatory 14-day admission, and group and cross-border frameworks.
assessmentNote: Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. THE CODE IS SCORED AGAINST ITS OWN STATED TERMS AND SPLITS ON THEM. Timeliness: failed on the stated standard - 713 days at March 2025 against a 330-day statutory cap including litigation, and worsening. Recovery: 30.56 per cent cumulative realisation at March 2026, falling year on year, with annual-flow realisation down to about 23 per cent in FY2025-26. Against the replaced regime, however, the behavioural effect is large and measured: 30,310 cases settled before admission covering defaults of 13.78 lakh crore to December 2024, which is the credible-threat effect working outside the courtroom, and Section 29A ended promoter buy-backs. Partly rests on that split - the deterrent works and the process does not meet its own clock or its own recovery expectations. ONE BENCHMARK DISPUTE IS LEFT OPEN RATHER THAN SETTLED: the case for holds that realisation should be read against liquidation value, at which it runs 167 per cent, and the case against reads it against admitted claims, at which the haircut is about 67 per cent. Both are computed from published figures; which is the fair denominator is a judgement this record does not make, and the verdict does not depend on choosing.
caseFor: The behavioural effect is the real achievement and it is large: 30,310 cases settled before admission, covering underlying defaults worth ₹13.78 lakh crore to December 2024. The credible threat of losing control transformed promoter behaviour in a way no previous recovery mechanism managed, and Section 29A permanently ended the practice of defaulting promoters buying back their own assets at a discount. Realisation percentages also understate performance, since the IBC inherited assets already stripped by years of delay under the old regime — realisation runs at 167% of liquidation value, which is the fairer benchmark.
caseAgainst: On its own stated terms it underdelivers. Timelines are more than double the statutory limit and worsening, realisation is low and declining monotonically as the best assets resolve first, and NCLT capacity has never matched caseload. A 67% average haircut means creditors recover a third of what they are owed, and the FY2026 collapse to 23% annual realisation suggests the trend is deteriorating rather than maturing. Pre-packaged insolvency for MSMEs, introduced in 2021, had admitted only 18 applications by March 2026.

shockExposure.why: Section 10A suspended fresh insolvency proceedings from March 2020 for the COVID period, creating a caseload gap and a subsequent backlog surge that distorts year-on-year comparisons across FY2021 and FY2022.

title: Loan write-offs and the recovery question
summary: Scheduled commercial banks wrote off ₹16,61,310 crore between April 2014 and September 2024 and recovered ₹2,69,795 crore against those write-offs — approximately 16%. Public sector banks accounted for ₹12,08,621 crore of the write-offs and recovered ₹2,16,547 crore.
whatHappened: Write-offs peaked in FY2018-19 at ₹2.36 lakh crore and have since declined to around ₹1.5-1.7 lakh crore annually. A substantial share of the headline decline in the gross NPA ratio from its 2018 peak is attributable to these write-offs and to credit growth expanding the denominator, alongside genuine recoveries which the RBI puts at around 42.8% of the FY2024-25 reduction.
caseFor: Write-offs are standard prudential practice once provisioning is complete; leaving fully provisioned bad loans on the books misrepresents a bank's position as much as concealing them does. Borrower liability is not extinguished and recovery proceedings continue, so the accounting entry and the legal claim are genuinely different things. Recoveries and upgrades now account for a rising share of NPA reduction, indicating the mechanism is shifting from write-off toward genuine resolution as the cycle matures.
caseAgainst: Recovery on written-off accounts runs at roughly 13-18% in practice, so for the overwhelming bulk of the amount the distinction between write-off and waiver is notional. The headline ratio improvement is therefore substantially cosmetic: ₹13.91 lakh crore remains unrecovered, absorbed by depositors and, through recapitalisation, by taxpayers. Presenting the fall from 14.58% to 1.8% as a cleanup without this context materially overstates what was achieved.

shockExposure.why: COVID forbearance suppressed reported NPAs across FY2021-FY2022, further complicating attribution of the decline between write-offs, recoveries, and forbearance unwinding.

sources.name: PIB, Building Trust: Strengthening India's banking sector

assessmentNote: Written 2026-08-05 (phase 15 batch 13); this record carried a `contested` verdict with no stated ground. THE TWO READINGS AGREE ON EVERY FACT AND DISAGREE ABOUT WHICH FRAME GOVERNS. Nobody disputes that recovery on written-off accounts runs at roughly 13-18 per cent, that Rs 13.91 lakh crore remains unrecovered, or that borrower liability survives the accounting entry. Reading one is PRUDENTIAL: a write-off after full provisioning is the correct treatment, the legal claim is untouched, and leaving fully provisioned assets on the books misstates a bank's position as surely as hiding them would. Reading two is ECONOMIC: at 13-18 per cent recovery the distinction between write-off and waiver is notional for the bulk of the amount, so a headline fall from 14.58 to 1.8 per cent presented as a cleanup overstates what happened, and the residue is borne by depositors and, through recapitalisation, taxpayers. THE RECORD DECLINES BECAUSE THE DISAGREEMENT IS NORMATIVE, NOT BECAUSE ANYTHING IS UNMEASURED. Both readings are simultaneously true of the same numbers; choosing between them would be choosing whether accounting correctness or economic incidence is the question, which is not a finding the evidence can settle. NOT a case of work left undone.
revisitTrigger: A published recovery series on written-off accounts by vintage would sharpen the second reading materially, but it would not settle the contest, because the disagreement is about which frame governs rather than about the rate.

title: PSB recapitalisation and consolidation
summary: Capital infusion of ₹3.31 lakh crore into public sector banks between FY2016-17 and FY2020-21, alongside consolidation reducing the number of PSBs from 27 to 12 through the SBI associate merger (2017), Bank of Baroda-Vijaya-Dena (2019), and the August 2019 mega-merger of 10 banks into 4 effective April 2020.
claimAtLaunch: Recapitalise banks to absorb recognised losses and resume lending; consolidate to create fewer, stronger, more efficient banks with national scale.
whatHappened: The October 2017 package of ₹2.11 lakh crore was the centrepiece, roughly ₹1.35 lakh crore of it through recapitalisation bonds. PSBs swung from a record aggregate loss of about ₹85,390 crore in FY2017-18 to record net profit of ₹1,78,364 crore in FY2024-25, up 26% year on year, with SBI contributing over 40%. No government infusion has been required since FY2020-21. PSB capital adequacy reached 16.4% by June 2025.
assessmentNote:
RESCORED FROM worked TO partly, 2026-08-06, on the ground two adversarial reviews reached independently and this instrument then confirmed: two objectives were announced and one is not established. Recapitalisation is evidenced; efficiency gains from consolidation, as distinct from the credit cycle and the rate environment, are not measured. There is no centrepiece exception and the note that explained the earlier choice documented a departure from the definition rather than authorising one. ON INDEPENDENCE: the qualifying source would be the RBI Financial Stability Report, whose CRAR series is the RBI’s own statutory publication and does bear on recapitalisation — but it is NOT HELD. Retrieval was attempted on 2026-08-06 through six named routes and failed at every one; see the crar series for the routes. The test is not passed on a document the instrument does not have.

PREVIOUS NOTE, PRESERVED VERBATIM: Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. TWO OBJECTIVES WERE ANNOUNCED AND THEY DO NOT RESOLVE THE SAME WAY. Recapitalisation: met decisively and measured - public-sector banks moved from an aggregate loss of about 85,390 crore in FY2017-18 to net profit of 1,78,364 crore in FY2024-25, capital adequacy reached 16.4 per cent by June 2025, and no government infusion has been required since FY2020-21. Five years without further capital is the strongest available evidence that the capital was adequate and correctly deployed. Consolidation: NOT established. The case against is that the profitability recovery tracks the credit cycle and rate environment rather than merger synergies, and that public-sector banks continued losing market share throughout; no evidence separating merger effects from cycle effects appears in this record and it is entered below as an absence. Worked is therefore asserted on the recapitalisation objective, which was the centrepiece and is decisively met, and NOT on consolidation. The fiscal opacity of the recapitalisation bonds - excluded from the headline deficit while adding to internal debt - is a criticism of the instrument's accounting, not of whether the banks were capitalised, and is left in the case against where it belongs.
caseFor: The fiscal and operational objective was met decisively. Banks absorbed recognised losses without a systemic failure, resumed lending, and reached self-sustaining profitability within seven years of a record loss — a turnaround few banking systems achieve after a crisis of that scale. That no further infusion has been needed for five years is the strongest evidence the capital was adequate and correctly deployed.
caseAgainst: Recapitalisation bonds were fiscally opaque: money raised was excluded from the headline fiscal deficit while adding to internal government debt, with a recurring interest cost, and in substance the government funded banks by borrowing from those same banks. Evidence that consolidation delivered its promised efficiency gains is thin — the profitability recovery tracks the credit cycle and rate environment more closely than merger synergies, and PSBs continued losing market share to private banks throughout.

shockExposure.why: The mega-merger took effect in April 2020, the same month as the COVID lockdown, making integration effects and pandemic effects impossible to separate cleanly.

unmeasured.what: Efficiency gains attributable to the bank mergers, as distinct from the credit cycle and rate environment
unmeasured.why: The consolidation half of the announced objective. The case against holds the evidence is thin and this record carries no measure separating merger synergies from cycle effects. Bank-level cost-to-income and productivity series exist, but no published study or official evaluation isolating the merger effect was retrieved.
unmeasured.wouldFill: An official post-merger evaluation, or bank-level efficiency series compared against a matched non-merged control.

title: IL&FS collapse
summary: Default by Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services, carrying ₹99,355 crore of total debt, triggering a liquidity freeze across the NBFC sector. The government superseded the board under a Uday Kotak-led team.
whatHappened: By June 2026, ₹50,387 crore had been discharged, about 82.6% of the ₹61,000 crore resolution target and roughly 61% of total external debt. Around 88.4% of the amount owed to public sector banks and financial institutions has been recovered — substantially above the average IBC recovery rate. The collapse was a major driver of the pre-COVID growth slowdown established in Phase 2.
caseFor: Board supersession rather than liquidation preserved going-concern value and produced recovery rates far above what the IBC route delivers, at 88.4% for bank creditors. The intervention was fast and prevented a disorderly cascade through the NBFC sector at a moment of acute fragility.
caseAgainst: The collapse itself represents a supervisory failure — a systemically important entity accumulated ₹99,355 crore of debt with an asset-liability mismatch that regulators did not act on until default. Resolution has taken eight years and remains incomplete. The credit freeze that followed contributed materially to the growth deceleration that preceded COVID.

shockExposure.why: CORRECTED 2026-08-06 on operator Rulings 6 and 7. WITHDRAWN WORDING, quoted so the correction can be checked rather than taken on trust: this field previously read "This record is itself a shock, and it lands inside the AQR credit squeeze, making the two effects on 2018-2020 credit conditions difficult to separate." The IL&FS default is a private company failing — neither an act of policy nor external to India — so Ruling 6 does not reach it, and Ruling 7 types the record by its subject, which is the failure itself and not the state’s response to it. The record is now typed event. WHAT SURVIVES THE RETYPE UNCHANGED: it lands inside the AQR credit squeeze, making the two effects on 2018-2020 credit conditions difficult to separate.

title: Yes Bank reconstruction and SMBC stake sale
summary: RBI-imposed moratorium and reconstruction scheme in March 2020, with an SBI-led consortium recapitalising the bank, culminating in the September 2025 sale of a 20% stake to Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation.
whatHappened: The reconstruction included writing off approximately ₹8,415 crore of Additional Tier 1 bonds, which triggered litigation — the Bombay High Court quashed the write-off and the matter proceeded to the Supreme Court. In September 2025 SMBC acquired 20% for ₹13,482 crore, buying 13.19% from SBI and 6.81% from seven private banks at ₹21.50 per share, valuing Yes Bank at around US$7.9 billion. The CCI cleared the transaction on 2 September 2025 and SMBC later raised its holding to 24.22%. It is the largest cross-border M&A transaction in India's financial sector.
caseFor: A private bank of systemic size was resolved without depositor loss and without permanent public ownership, and the state-led consortium exited at a profit into a credible foreign strategic investor five years later. That is close to the textbook outcome for a bank rescue, and compares favourably with resolutions in far wealthier jurisdictions.
caseAgainst: The AT-1 bond write-off damaged trust in a funding instrument the entire banking system relies on, and the courts have not vindicated the regulator's approach — the Bombay High Court quashed it. The bank reached that condition under RBI supervision, so the rescue's success does not offset the supervisory failure that made it necessary.
assessmentNote: Rescored from worked to no-objective on 2026-08-03 after retrieval failed. The objective is named and has not been read: the Yes Bank Limited Reconstruction Scheme, 2020, notified by the Central Government vide G.S.R. 174(E) of 13 March 2020 under sub-sections (4) and (7) of section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949. The gazette was not obtained - only a private portal's reproduction of it - so no score against the scheme is supportable, and worked was resting on an objective nobody in this project has read. The reproduction's paragraph structure carries no objects clause at all, which if confirmed against the gazette would mean the scheme states no objective to score against in the first place. Revisit on retrieval: confirm, and if the scheme does state an object, rescore against it.
differentFactsNote: The government's case rests on the financial outcome: no depositor loss, no permanent public ownership, and a profitable exit into a strategic investor. The critics' case rests on a judicial determination that the AT-1 write-off was unlawful, and on the supervision that made the rescue necessary. No measure places a court's ruling on legality and a return on capital on one ledger.

shockExposure.why: The moratorium landed weeks before the COVID lockdown, so the recovery period coincides entirely with pandemic-era monetary support, which flatters the outcome.

title: Digital public infrastructure: Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, UPI
summary: The JAM stack — Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana bank accounts, Aadhaar identity, and mobile connectivity — underpinning Direct Benefit Transfer and the Unified Payments Interface.
claimAtLaunch: Universal bank account access, elimination of ghost and duplicate welfare beneficiaries through biometric authentication, and a public payments rail owned by no private intermediary.
whatHappened: 56.77 crore Jan Dhan accounts by October 2025, holding ₹2.73 lakh crore, 56% held by women and 66% rural or semi-urban. UPI grew from 535 crore transactions worth ₹8.77 lakh crore in FY2018-19 to 24,162 crore transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore in FY2025-26, around 85% of India's retail digital payments, with India accounting for roughly 49% of global real-time payment volume. ₹6.9 lakh crore was transferred via Jan Dhan accounts in FY2024-25 alone.
assessmentNote:
RESCORED FROM worked TO partly, 2026-08-06. Three objectives were announced: universal account access, elimination of ghost and duplicate beneficiaries through biometric authentication, and a public payments rail. Two are evidenced. The third is not measured at all, and neither is its counterpart — eligible people excluded by authentication failure — so the record cannot say whether the deduplication removed ghosts, claimants, or both. ON INDEPENDENCE: UPI volumes are published by NPCI as a routine function and would qualify, but this record reaches them through a news account of the Financial Stability Report rather than through NPCI, and the account is T4. Account counts come from the scheme’s own portal, which is the announcing body.

PREVIOUS NOTE, PRESERVED VERBATIM: Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. THREE OBJECTIVES WERE ANNOUNCED; TWO ARE MEASURED AND MET, AND THE THIRD IS THE ONE THE CASE AGAINST IS ABOUT. Account access: 56.77 crore Jan Dhan accounts by October 2025, 56 per cent held by women and 66 per cent rural or semi-urban, with adult account ownership rising from 53 per cent in 2014 to near-universal. A public payments rail: UPI at 24,162 crore transactions worth 314 lakh crore in FY2025-26, about 85 per cent of retail digital payments, owned by no private intermediary. Both met on their own terms and at a scale no comparable country has matched. ELIMINATION OF GHOST AND DUPLICATE BENEFICIARIES - the third announced objective - IS NOT MEASURED HERE, and neither is its cost. The case against records documented authentication failures denying rations to the elderly, manual labourers and the disabled; this record carries no count of either the duplicates removed or the eligible people excluded, and both are entered below. Worked is asserted on the two measured objectives. It is NOT a finding that the system excluded nobody, and the exclusion question is live and unquantified in this record.
caseFor: This is the clearest and most internationally consequential achievement of the period. India built payments and identity infrastructure as a public good rather than a private oligopoly, at a scale and cost no comparable country has matched, and it is now actively emulated abroad. Account ownership rose from 53% of adults in 2014 to near-universal, and the COVID transfer response would have been impossible without the rails already in place.
caseAgainst: Exclusion is the cost the headline figures hide: biometric authentication failures have produced documented denials of rations and entitlements, falling hardest on the elderly, manual labourers and the disabled — precisely those the system was meant to reach. The Aadhaar Act was passed as a money bill, bypassing the Rajya Sabha, and the Supreme Court struck down Section 57 in 2018. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 grants broad government exemptions, so the surveillance capacity this infrastructure creates remains largely unconstrained. Zero-MDR drove UPI adoption but eliminated the payment industry's revenue base, leaving the rails dependent on state support.
differentFactsNote: The government's case rests on coverage: account ownership from 53 per cent of adults to near-universal, and a transfer capability the COVID response depended on. The critics' case rests on authentication failures denying entitlements, and on the constitutional route - passage as a money bill, Section 57 struck down, and the exemptions the 2023 Act grants. Exclusion counts could in principle net against coverage; the constitutional facts cannot share a ledger with account ownership.

shockExposure.why: COVID accelerated digital adoption globally, so part of the UPI growth curve reflects a worldwide shift rather than India-specific policy — though India's starting infrastructure is what allowed it to capitalise.

unmeasured.what: Eligible beneficiaries denied entitlements through biometric authentication failure
unmeasured.why: The case against rests on documented denials and this record carries no count. Authentication failure rates are held by the scheme operators and the identity authority; a count of resulting denials by scheme, and of what happened to those people, has not been released in any form retrieved.
unmeasured.wouldFill: Scheme-level authentication-failure and fallback-exception data, or an official audit of exclusion under biometric authentication.

unmeasured.what: Ghost and duplicate beneficiaries actually removed, as distinct from savings claimed
unmeasured.why: The elimination of ghost and duplicate beneficiaries was an announced objective. Figures circulate as claimed savings rather than as counts of duplicates identified and removed, and the two are different quantities; no count on a stated basis was retrieved. Entered 2026-08-05 when the assessment note was written and the objective was found to be unscored.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A scheme-level statement from the Department of Food and Public Distribution, the Ministry of Rural Development or the Unique Identification Authority giving beneficiaries deleted as duplicates and as non-existent, separately, by scheme and year - the holders run the deduplication and produce the counts internally.

sources.name: PIB, Building Trust: Strengthening India's banking sector

title: Public sector bank privatisation programme
summary: Budget 2021-22 announced the intent to privatise two public sector banks alongside the strategic sale of IDBI Bank.
claimAtLaunch: Reduce the state's footprint in banking and improve efficiency by transferring two PSBs to private ownership.
whatHappened: Five years on, no public sector bank has been privatised. The IDBI Bank strategic sale — the government's 30.48% plus LIC's 30.24%, totalling 60.72% — advanced through FY2025-26 with revised bids from Fairfax Financial Holdings and Emirates NBD under evaluation by mid-2026, valued at around US$5.7 billion and targeted for FY27. No legislation enabling broader PSB privatisation has been introduced.
assessmentNote: Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. FAILED IS ASSERTED ON DELIVERY AGAINST A SPECIFIC ANNOUNCED COMMITMENT, AND ON NOTHING ELSE. Two public sector banks were to be privatised. Five years on none has been, no enabling legislation has been introduced, and the one live transaction is IDBI Bank - which the government's own classification does not count as a public sector bank for this purpose, and which was still at bid-evaluation stage in mid-2026. A commitment announced in a Budget speech, left formally alive and not acted on, is the announced-but-not-delivered shape this project records as failure. THE MERITS OF PRIVATISING ARE NOT SCORED. The case for is that the rationale weakened on its own terms once the banks returned to profitability and full capital adequacy without a sale, and that restraint may be judgement rather than failure of will. This record does not adjudicate that; it records that the stated intention was neither delivered nor withdrawn. A reader who thinks the policy was wrong should read this verdict as being about the commitment, not about the policy.
caseFor: The rationale weakened on its own merits: PSBs returned to record profitability and full capital adequacy without privatisation, so the urgency that motivated the announcement dissolved. Selling recovering assets into a weak market would have destroyed value, and the IDBI process advancing to final bids shows the capability exists where the case is strong. Restraint here may reflect judgment rather than failure of will.
caseAgainst: A specific commitment announced in a Budget speech has gone unfulfilled for five years, with no enabling legislation even attempted. The political cost of bank-union opposition, not the economics, is the widely understood reason. If the intent was abandoned it should have been stated; leaving it formally alive while doing nothing is the pattern this project should record as announced-but-not-delivered.

shockExposure.why: None material — the announcement postdates COVID's acute phase and the delay spans a period of banking-sector strength.

sources.name: PIB, Gross NPAs reduce from 9.11% to 2.58%

title: Credit composition shift toward unsecured retail
summary: Bank credit shifted structurally away from industry and infrastructure toward retail and personal lending, with unsecured retail rising from 22.9% to 25.2% of the retail book and retail loans growing at roughly 24.8% CAGR between FY21 and FY23, about double overall credit growth.
whatHappened: The RBI raised risk weights on unsecured consumer credit from 100% to 125% in November 2023 and added 25 percentage points to bank lending to NBFCs, partially rolling this back in February 2025 while retaining the 125% on unsecured retail. By FY2025-26 credit growth of 14.5% outpaced deposit growth of 11.5%, and the RBI flagged unsecured retail, microfinance stress and the credit-deposit gap as the system's principal vulnerabilities.
caseFor: This is healthy diversification away from the concentrated corporate and infrastructure exposures that caused the last crisis. Granular retail risk is more predictable than lumpy project finance, and the expansion reflects genuine financial deepening in an under-banked economy where credit to the private sector is only around 55% of GDP, far below peers.
caseAgainst: It may be risk migration rather than risk reduction — the next crisis would be a household one, and the RBI has noted roughly 10% of retail borrowers missing payments. Deposit growth persistently lagging credit growth is the classic precondition for funding stress, and the fact that the regulator needed to raise risk weights and has only partially reversed them indicates supervisory discomfort rather than confidence.

shockExposure.why: Post-COVID consumption recovery inflated retail credit demand, so part of the growth reflects a normalising base rather than a structural shift.

title: Bank frauds and supervisory detection
summary: A sequence of very large frauds detected during the period: Punjab National Bank / Nirav Modi and Mehul Choksi (₹14,357 crore, detected 2018), ABG Shipyard (₹22,842 crore, 2022, the largest in Indian banking history, across 28 banks), DHFL (₹34,615 crore, 2022), and Vijay Mallya / Kingfisher (around ₹9,000 crore across 17 banks).
whatHappened: Aggregate fraud value doubled to ₹1.85 trillion in FY2020, then frauds above ₹100 crore declined sharply to ₹41,000 crore in FY2022 from ₹1.05 trillion in FY2021. The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018 created a framework to attach absconders' assets. The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act 2020 brought co-operative banks under RBI supervision following the PMC Bank collapse.
caseFor: The enforcement architecture was genuinely strengthened — the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, co-operative bank supervision, and improved reporting all postdate 2014 and address real gaps. That the frauds surfaced at all reflects the same recognition discipline the AQR imposed; under the previous regime several would likely have remained buried in restructured accounts.
caseAgainst: Every one of these frauds was detected years after it began, which is a supervisory failure rather than a detection success — the PNB fraud ran through SWIFT for years undetected. Governance reform through the Banks Board Bureau and its successor has thin evidence of improving board quality or appointment processes. Both principal fugitives remain outside Indian jurisdiction years after the framework designed to reach them was enacted.

sources.name: PIB, Building Trust: Strengthening India's banking sector

title: Expected Credit Loss provisioning transition
summary: RBI final directions issued 27 April 2026 mandate a shift from incurred-loss to expected-credit-loss provisioning effective 1 April 2027, with a glide path to March 2031. The one-time capital impact is not established here: the only figure in circulation is a T4 relay and no primary source for it has been retrieved.
caseFor: The transition is announced with a long lead and a stated timetable: directions issued 27 April 2026, effective 1 April 2027, phased to March 2031. Banks have the rule and the dates years before either binds, which is the opposite of the recognition discipline this system has had imposed on it before - retrospectively, at supervisory speed, on balance sheets already carrying the losses. A standing forward-looking rule also removes the discretion that overdue-ageing recognition leaves in the gap between a loan going bad and a bank saying so.
caseAgainst: It is a forward-dated comparability break on every asset-quality series it touches, which is why it exists in this instrument as provenance record P-21 as well as here: crar and net-npa will step at the transition for a reason that is not a change in asset quality. A four-year phase-in is also four years in which the timing of recognition is a choice rather than a rule, and the transition lands while those same series are being read as evidence that the last cleanup finished. On this record none of that can be sized: the directions themselves have never been retrieved and the only quantified impact in circulation is a T4 relay.
